title: QuantumScience Claw: a correct calculation is only part of the story
summary: What happens when a local AI agent can run real quantum software—and we check what it actually did?
announcement: Ongoing research · Led by Ethan Seefried & Tirthankar Ghosal

sections.heading: A plausible answer is not a scientific result
sections.body: Imagine asking an assistant to prepare a quantum state. It returns a convincing circuit diagram. Did that circuit actually prepare the right state? Was anything simulated? And did the final answer include the verified artifact? QuantumScience Claw (QSC), led by Ethan Seefried and Tirthankar Ghosal, investigates those questions by connecting a local AI agent to real quantum error-correction software.

sections.heading: Let the scientific tools do the scientific work
sections.body: Quantum error correction encodes information across physical qubits so errors can be detected and corrected. Many tasks have precise checks: circuit constraints, stabilizer properties, and simulation counts. QSC uses a local Muse Glimmer 30B model through llama.cpp, OpenClaw as its runtime, selected MIT ScienceClaw components, and controlled operations through the QHPC Ecosystem (EQO). Established software—including Stim, Sinter, and PyMatching—performs the calculations. The model coordinates their use; it does not replace their algorithms.

sections.heading: Three finish lines, not one
sections.body: Think of a laboratory test: running the instrument, passing a quality check, and delivering the result to the researcher are different events. QSC separates execution, scientific verification, and accepted final submission in the same way. On 192 StabilizerBench B1 tasks spanning 14 code families, the complete system finished 129 within a 300-second deadline per task. Among the remaining 63, twelve passed verification without an accepted submission, two reached the verifier without passing, and 49 had no recorded official verifier call.

sections.heading: The number needs its context
sections.body: The deterministic circuit-synthesis backend can solve these benchmark instances directly. QSC also exposes a specialized Stim synthesis operation that the comparison configurations do not receive in the same form. The experiment therefore shows the capability of the complete agent-plus-tools system. It does not isolate a causal benefit from orchestration, or show that a language model improved the underlying synthesis algorithm. The unfinished tasks make the next research problem concrete: turn available scientific capability into reliable task completion.

sections.heading: From circuits to evidence-driven experiments
sections.body: The numerical campaign extends beyond circuit generation: algebra, code parameters, surface-code memory simulations, decoder compatibility, selected measured data, and limited external-artifact reproduction. In one adaptive episode, the agent used intermediate evidence to meet six precision targets below the allowed 49,152-shot budget, while a trusted controller enforced budgets and uncertainty calculations. That is an encouraging evidence-driven loop—not a controlled demonstration of superior sampling efficiency.

sections.heading: Sometimes the right answer is no conclusion
sections.body: A larger study ran 1.2 million shots across 24 configurations. Its fit failed the prespecified goodness-of-fit test, so the system did not accept a threshold estimate. Failure handling exposes another gap: the infrastructure detected all seven injected faults, but the agent completed the failure-reporting protocol in only two cases, improving to three with explicit guidance. Preventing invalid results and communicating failure are separate capabilities.

sections.heading: Keep the receipts—and mind the overhead
sections.body: Evidence replay reconstructed all 68 recorded numerical-campaign outcomes in the pinned environment, including unsuccessful episodes. This is auditability, not independent replication. On the local DGX GB10 deployment, median inference requests took 22.7 seconds, worker processes 0.49 seconds, and complete episodes about 134 seconds. These have different denominators and cannot be added into a precise runtime breakdown. They nevertheless motivate attention to coordination overhead.

sections.heading: The next milestone is reliable completion
sections.body: The team is investigating the unfinished benchmark cases, deadline sensitivity, matched access to synthesis algorithms, and better scientific interfaces. The broader lesson is simple: scientific agents need appropriate tools, checks independent of generated text, preserved evidence, and a reliable final handoff. QuantumScience Claw is ongoing research into that full chain—not a claim of unrestricted autonomous discovery.

title: SafeLens: reading between the safety records
summary: A near-miss report is one observation. Hundreds of thousands of reports can become organizational memory—if we know how to ask useful questions.

sections.heading: The signal is already there
sections.body: Imagine three reports written months apart: a crowded walkway, equipment blocking access, and a near miss during a delivery. Individually, each deserves attention. Together, they might reveal a recurring problem. This illustrative example captures the challenge: organizations have the observations, but connecting them takes work.

sections.heading: A count tells you how much—not what to investigate
sections.body: SafeLens analyzes a collection of 468,397 safety records spanning 11 years. A chart can show an increase in observations; the descriptions explain what people actually noticed. The system combines fast, deterministic statistics with AI analysis on demand, helping reviewers move from an organizational overview to a particular building, period, or interaction type. [1]

sections.heading: Four layers, one practical workflow
sections.body: First, records are cleaned and stored in a compact Parquet file. Second, filters produce the relevant slice and its statistics. Third, a representative sample goes to a language model, which returns ranked risks, recurring patterns, and good practices. Finally, a dashboard lets users inspect insights, browse records, ask follow-up questions, and export a report. Think of it as a librarian who narrows the shelf before helping you read. [1]

sections.heading: Why sampling deserves a starring role
sections.body: A model cannot reliably read the entire archive at once. But a random handful may miss uncommon record types. SafeLens uses Stratified Adaptive Query Sampling (SAQS): divide records by their existing interaction-type labels, allocate slots proportionally with a minimum floor, and sample within each group. The default budget is 300 records. This aims to preserve category diversity; it does not guarantee finding every rare hazard. Field observations and safety conversations also remain distinguishable, because they describe different kinds of evidence. [1]

sections.heading: An insight is an invitation to look closer
sections.body: The interface presents risky behaviors, common patterns, and best practices side by side. Each insight includes context and a supporting excerpt. Reviewers can return to individual records or ask a follow-up question. In the paper’s usage discussion, managers treat the ranked list as an agenda for investigation, sometimes promoting an item that their domain knowledge makes important. The useful outcome is a better-informed review, with the human still deciding what warrants action. [1]

sections.heading: What the deployment reports
sections.body: Across 136 evaluation runs, the paper reports an average response time of 19.49 seconds and a 6.6% system error rate. All 20 explicit feedback submissions were positive. Its definition of an error includes blank outputs, disrupted workflows, and freezes; it is not a measure of factual error in generated insights. [1]

sections.heading: Encouraging evidence, with clear boundaries
sections.body: Twenty positive ratings are useful early feedback, not proof of universal satisfaction or factual accuracy. The study reports a deployed demonstration rather than a controlled test of accident reduction. Its strongest practical lesson is that filtering, sampling, traceable excerpts, and expert review matter alongside the language model. Future work includes token-aware sampling and stronger handling of institution-specific terminology. [1]

title: BLUEPRINT: finding the right drawing in a mountain of records
summary: A drawing is more than its filename. BLUEPRINT connects what a page says, where it says it, and what an engineer needs to find.

sections.heading: The drawing exists. Finding it is the problem.
sections.body: Imagine inheriting a workshop with decades of binders. You need the electrical schematic for one panel and the procedure that goes with it. A filename tells you little; the clue might be a tiny identifier in a corner. Searching every page by hand is like looking for a book when the catalogue has lost its labels.

sections.heading: Read the page like an engineer
sections.body: BLUEPRINT first separates drawings from text documents. For drawings, it locates useful regions—such as title blocks and parts lists—and reads those crops. For documents, it extracts text. It combines exact-term and meaning-based search, then reranks matches using regional evidence. [1]

sections.heading: What changed in the results?
sections.body: Table 3 evaluates 375 queries on a 5,000-file benchmark. BLUEPRINT achieves 71.5% Success@3 versus 62.3% for LLaMA 3.2 Vision: a 9.2-percentage-point increase. Its nDCG@3 is 0.626 versus 0.521. Success@3 asks whether a relevant result appears in the first three hits; nDCG also rewards ordering. [1]

sections.heading: Why it matters
sections.body: A useful search system should lead an engineer to the evidence they can inspect. Better localization and OCR remain opportunities for improvement. The operational records are not publicly releasable; the paper discusses a separate unrestricted benchmark. [1]

title: From operational records to evidence-backed intelligence
summary: How retrieval, agentic reasoning, and expert oversight come together in AI for Laboratory Operations.

sections.heading: Start with the evidence
sections.body: Laboratory operations draw on engineering records, safety observations, policies, and procedures. AI for Laboratory Operations connects these sources with tools for discovery, safety analysis, and governance.

sections.heading: Different questions, connected research
sections.body: BLUEPRINT investigates multimodal retrieval for engineering drawings. SafeLens explores organizational safety records for actionable insights. REFSafE focuses on grounded risk analysis and safety reporting, while ORCHID supports policy-grounded classification of high-risk property.

sections.heading: Built with operational expertise
sections.body: The research team works with ORNL Operations collaborators, subject-matter experts, and ITSD software colleagues. Their involvement connects scientific methods with the practical needs of operational users.

title: Trustworthy analytics for HPC operations
summary: Introducing two research directions in multi-agent operational analytics and telemetry-informed decisions.

sections.heading: Beyond retrieving the right records
sections.body: Recall Is Not Honesty examines multi-agent architectures for trustworthy HPC operational analytics. The work has been accepted at SC ’26, as reported by the research team.

sections.heading: Toward defensible decisions
sections.body: EPIC++ is ongoing research into decentralized multi-agent analytics for job submission decisions on HPC telemetry. It explores how operational evidence can support defensible choices.

sections.heading: Research across institutions
sections.body: The supplied author teams connect Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Predii, Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, spinTwo, Rensselaer Polytechnic Institute, and AMD.
